title: Post-dural puncture headache (post-LP) and epidural blood patch
presentation: Headache or neurologic symptoms, often relieved lying flat, within 5 days of a neuraxial procedure — suspect PDPH
Often neck stiffness and subjective hearing symptoms; also spinal pain, visual disturbance, vertigo
Higher risk: younger adults and women (high certainty); prior headache history (moderate)
definitions: ICHD-3 (as summarized by the consensus): headache within 5 days of LP from CSF leak, usually with neck stiffness or hearing symptoms, remitting within 2 weeks or after the leak is sealed
Consensus caveats: onset can be >5 days; a postural component is usually present; the puncture may go unnoticed; headache can outlast 2 weeks

immediateActions.action: Confirm timing and postural pattern; check for imaging triggers (workup)
Oral hydration (IV only if oral not possible); scheduled acetaminophen + NSAID unless contraindicated; caffeine in the first 24 h of symptoms (≤900 mg/day)
Short-term opioid may be considered; occipital nerve block may be offered after spinal with a ≥22 G needle

immediateActions.window: Refractory and impairing ADLs, or severe neuro symptoms

immediateActions.action: Follow until headache resolves; urgent imaging if worse after EBP, new focal deficit, or headache changes

indication: Non-orthostatic headache, or orthostatic headache that becomes non-orthostatic
Focal deficit, visual change, altered consciousness or seizure (especially postpartum)
Worsening despite EBP, new focal symptoms or change in headache
notes: Alternatives to exclude include subdural hematoma and CVST
Routine imaging before EBP: insufficient evidence (statement, low certainty)

workup.test: Antithrombotic review, platelet count and temperature before EBP
notes: Follow neuraxial antithrombotic guidance — see vascular-antithrombotics:periprocedural-holds-lp-evd (B, moderate)
Pregnancy: platelets ≥70,000/µL with normal function and coagulation → low epidural hematoma risk (statement, moderate)
Fever or systemic infection: caution; deferring EBP may be appropriate (C, moderate)

treatment.doseText: Maintain oral hydration; IV fluids only when oral intake can't be maintained
Temporizing symptom relief only — not routine treatment
evidenceNote: Uppal 2023: grade C, low certainty (routine use not supported)

treatment.doseText: Scheduled, unless contraindicated (source gives no doses)
First 24 h of symptoms; max 900 mg/day (200–300 mg/day if breastfeeding); avoid multiple sources
notes: Evidence from 2 small RCTs; excess can cause withdrawal, dehydration, seizures

treatment.doseText: May consider short-term if multimodal analgesia fails; no long-term use
evidenceNote: Uppal 2023: short-term grade C, low certainty; long-term grade D, moderate certainty

treatment.doseText: May offer after spinal anesthesia with a narrower (≥22 G) needle (source gives no volume)
notes: Headache may recur; more severe headache may still need EBP
Benefit after wider-gauge punctures unclear (statement, low certainty)

treatment.doseText: Autologous blood, usually 15–20 mL (optimal volume unknown; >30 mL adds nothing), at or one level below the puncture; inject slowly and stop for significant back pain or headache
notes: Indications: refractory to conservative care and impairing ADLs (B, moderate); severe neurologic symptoms such as hearing loss or cranial neuropathy (C, moderate)
Within 48 h of dural puncture: counsel that a repeat EBP is more likely (B, moderate)
Complete relief 33–91% in recent series (statement, low)
Consent: repeat dural puncture, backache, neurologic complications (A, high)
Strict asepsis (B); no routine blood cultures (D, low)
Image guidance (fluoroscopy/CT, transforaminal) individualized — e.g., prior laminectomy or failed interlaminar EBP (C, moderate)
Persistent, worsening or changed backache after EBP → look for another diagnosis (C, low)
Prior EBP shouldn't stop future epidural analgesia (C, low)
evidenceNote: Uppal 2023: grade B, moderate certainty (EBP when refractory and impairing ADLs)
Volume and success figures: ungraded consensus statements (low; >30 mL moderate)

treatment.doseText: Hydrocortisone, theophylline, triptans, ACTH/cosyntropin, neostigmine/atropine, piritramide, methylergonovine, gabapentin — evidence doesn't support routine use
SPG block, acupuncture, epidural dextran/gelatin/hydroxyethyl starch, routine fibrin glue — evidence doesn't support routine use
notes: Fibrin glue: reserve for EBP-refractory PDPH or when EBP is contraindicated; anaphylaxis and aseptic meningitis reported
Epidural saline: temporary benefit at most (statement, low)

pitfalls: No routine prophylactic EBP after dural puncture (I, low), no prophylactic bed rest (D, moderate), no routine prophylactic drugs or neuraxial injections (I, low)

Your own LPs: use noncutting (atraumatic) needles in all populations (A, high); if cutting, narrower gauge (A, high) with the bevel parallel to the spine's long axis (B, moderate); lateral decubitus and fewer attempts are associated with lower risk (statements, moderate)
Long-term associations: chronic headache, back/neck pain, depression, cranial nerve palsy, SDH, CVST (moderate); unknown whether EBP prevents them
Hand off: tell the primary team/PCP about the PDPH and arrange follow-up until resolution (B, moderate)
escalateWhen: Worsening despite EBP, new focal neurologic symptoms, or change in headache character → urgent neuroimaging and specialist referral (B, moderate)
Focal deficit, visual change, altered consciousness or seizure → neuroimaging for an alternative diagnosis (B, moderate)
institutionVaries: Who performs EBP (anesthesia vs interventional radiology) and with what image guidance
Post-LP follow-up pathway (consensus: centers doing LPs should have one)
sources: Uppal V, et al. Consensus practice guidelines on postdural puncture headache from a multisociety, international working group: a summary report. JAMA Netw Open 2023;6(8):e2325387. doi:10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2023.25387
